<reason>A more convincingly defends a bounded, rebuttable family priority. It includes residents’ relational interests within the public interest, answers chain-migration concerns with dependency limits, and allows substantial public harm to override reunification. B correctly distinguishes integration from economic contribution, but A explicitly accommodates that distinction. B’s chosen-versus-imposed-cost argument remains competitive, yet does not establish why ordinary fiscal advantages generally outweigh continued separation. Its closing also calls family eligibility expandable without adequately addressing A’s stated limits.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A directly answers B’s claim that economic exceptions destroy family priority: a presumption is not an absolute entitlement. B’s subsequent parent-child exception reinforces that distinction without conceding the entire motion. On the remaining scope dispute, calling spousal and caregiving separation “queuing” does little to answer A’s account of irreplaceable relational losses.</best_rebuttal>
